title: Gravitation
summary: Newton's law of gravitation, g, Kepler's laws, and satellites.
cards.0.p: Every object with mass attracts other objects, and the force is F = G·m1·m2/r2. Here r is the distance between the centers of the two objects. G is a very small number.
cards.0.svg#5: r: distance from center to center
cards.0.key: G is about 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². r is the distance between the centers, not between the surfaces.
cards.0.once.soru: Does the friend sitting next to you attract you?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Every object with mass attracts. G is so small that you cannot feel this force.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Gravity is not only for planets. Every mass attracts.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Gravity acts at a distance. No contact is needed.
cards.1.p: The force is proportional to the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance. If the distance doubles, the force drops to 1/4. If it triples, the force drops to 1/9.
cards.1.key: If one of the masses doubles, the force doubles. If the distance is cut in half, the force becomes 4 times larger.
cards.2.p: Two objects attract each other with forces of the same magnitude in opposite directions. The accelerations come from a = F/m. An apple falls at 9.8 m/s², while Earth's acceleration is about 10−25 m/s².
cards.2.svg#0: equal magnitude, opposite direction, different objects
cards.2.key: This is Newton's third law. The forces are equal, but the accelerations are not. The object with less mass accelerates more.
cards.3.p: Every mass creates a gravitational field around it, and g = F/m. That gives g = G·M/r2. g does not depend on the mass of the falling object, and at the surface it is about 9.8 m/s².
cards.3.key: The gravitational field is the gravitational force per unit mass. g depends only on the planet's mass (M) and the distance from its center (r).
cards.3.once.soru: If a planet kept the same mass but had half the radius, what would g at its surface be?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: Since g = GM/r², halving r makes r² one quarter as large, so g becomes 4 times larger.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: g is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, not to the distance.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: The mass is the same, but the surface is closer to the center. g depends on distance.
cards.4.h: g is not the same everywhere
cards.4.p: g gets smaller as you move away from the center, and on the Moon g is about 1.6 m/s². Your mass (kg) is the same everywhere. Your weight (N) equals m·g, so it changes from place to place.
cards.4.svg#9: m = 50 kg: weight 490 N on Earth, ≈ 80 N on the Moon
cards.4.key: If you rise a height R above the ground, r = 2R and g drops to one quarter (≈ 2.45 m/s²).
cards.4.etk.soru: Rise above the ground. How do g and your weight change? (Earth's radius ≈ 6370 km)
cards.5.p: Planets move around the Sun in elliptical orbits, with the Sun at one focus of the ellipse. The point closest to the Sun is the perihelion, and the farthest point is the aphelion.
cards.5.svg#5: 1st law: the orbit is an ellipse
cards.5.svg#6: real orbits are very close to circles (drawing exaggerated)
cards.5.key: The Sun is at one focus of the ellipse, not at its center. Earth's orbit is almost a circle.
cards.5.once.soru: What is the shape of Earth's orbit around the Sun?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Earth's orbit is an ellipse that is very close to a circle, with the Sun at one focus.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: The orbit is close to a circle, but not exactly one. The distance changes a little over the year.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: The orbit is closed, and Earth does not fall into the Sun.
cards.6.p: Kepler's second law explains why a planet speeds up at perihelion. It says the line joining the Sun and the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. The seasons, though, come from the tilt of the axis, not from the distance.
cards.6.svg#4: areas swept in equal times are equal
cards.6.key: This law comes from the conservation of angular momentum (L = m·r·v⊥). Earth reaches perihelion in early January, when it is winter in the northern hemisphere.
cards.7.p: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the average distance, so T²/r³ = constant. The constant depends on the mass at the center. A distant planet has a longer year.
cards.7.key: r is the semi-major axis of the ellipse. The constant is the same only for objects orbiting the same central body.
cards.7.etk.soru: The farther from the Sun, the longer the year. Put the planets in order of orbital period, from shortest to longest.
cards.7.once.soru: A planet is 4 times farther from the Sun than Earth. How many Earth years long is its year?
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: The period is not directly proportional to the distance.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: 16 is 4². But it is the cube of the distance that is proportional to the square of the period.
cards.8.h: A satellite: an object that is always falling
cards.8.p: The force that keeps a satellite in orbit is gravity. From G·M·m/r² = m·v²/r we get v = √(G·M/r). The satellite's mass cancels, and the lower the orbit, the higher the speed.
cards.8.svg#7: orbital speed does not depend on the satellite's mass
cards.8.key: Gravity acts as the centripetal force (see Circular and rotational motion). A heavy satellite and a light one in the same orbit move at the same speed.
cards.9.p: A satellite whose period equals Earth's rotation period (24 hours) is called geosynchronous. If it orbits above the equator, it is called geostationary. At a height of about 36 000 km, it always stays above the same point.
cards.9.svg#0: view from above the North Pole (not to scale)
cards.9.key: A geostationary satellite moves in a circular orbit in the same direction as Earth's rotation. TV and communication satellites work this way. A circular orbit with a 24-hour period has only one possible radius.
cards.9.once.soru: Why does a satellite dish on a roof always point the same way without ever being turned?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: The satellite goes around once every 24 hours. It turns at the same rate as Earth, so it looks fixed in the sky.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: If the satellite stood still, it would fall to Earth. It actually moves at about 3 km per second.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.yazi: The signal comes from every direction
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: The signal comes from one satellite, and the dish has to face it.
cards.10.p: On the space station (about 400 km up), g is still about 8.7 m/s², so gravity is there. The station and the astronaut are in free fall together. That is why a scale reads 0.
cards.10.svg#2: at ≈ 400 km, gravity is not gone
cards.10.svg#3: the station and the astronaut fall freely together
cards.10.svg#4: the scale reads 0 → feeling of weightlessness
cards.10.key: Thanks to their sideways speed, the station and the astronaut keep missing Earth. Weightlessness is free fall, not the absence of gravity.
cards.11.p: The minimum speed needed to break free of a planet's gravity and never come back is the escape velocity: v = √(2·G·M/R). For Earth it is about 11.2 km/s.
cards.11.key: Escape velocity does not depend on the object's mass. It is √2 times the orbital speed near the surface (from 7.9 km/s to 11.2 km/s).
cards.12.h: The energy of a satellite in orbit
cards.12.p: Gravitational potential energy is Eₚ = −G·M·m/r, and it is zero at infinity. The total energy in orbit is E = −G·M·m/(2r). A satellite that moves lower speeds up, but its total energy decreases.
cards.12.key: Eₚ is negative because it decreases as the objects get closer, and KE = G·M·m/(2r). In a bound orbit E < 0. Also KE = −E and Eₚ = 2E.
cards.12.once.soru: A satellite drops to a lower orbit. What happens to its speed?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: Since v = √(GM/r), the speed goes up when r gets smaller.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: Gravity is stronger lower down. To stay in orbit, the satellite has to move faster.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: Orbital speed depends on the radius.
cards.13.p: The Moon's pull is stronger on the side of Earth facing the Moon and weaker on the far side. This difference creates two bulges of water. That is why the sea rises twice a day on most coasts.
cards.13.svg#6: the near side is pulled more, the far side less
cards.13.svg#7: most coasts: 2 high + 2 low tides a day (exaggerated)
cards.13.key: On the near side the water is pulled toward the Moon, and on the far side it is left behind. Tides come from the difference in gravity with distance, not from gravity itself.
cards.13.once.soru: On most coasts, how many times a day does the sea rise?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: There is a bulge on each side of Earth. As Earth turns, every coast passes through both.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: There is a bulge on the far side too, not only on the side facing the Moon.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: There are two bulges. One is on the side facing the Moon, the other on the opposite side.
cards.14.p:
• The gravitational force is F = G·m₁·m₂/r², and when r doubles F drops to one quarter.
• g = G·M/r². It is about 9.8 m/s² at the surface and 1.6 m/s² on the Moon.
• Kepler's laws: elliptical orbits, equal areas, and T² ∝ r³.
• For a satellite v = √(G·M/r), and weightlessness is free fall.
• Earth's escape velocity is 11.2 km/s.
quiz.0.q: The gravitational force between two objects is 90 N. If the distance between them is tripled and one of the masses is doubled, what is the new force, in N?
quiz.0.e: The force is proportional to mass and inversely proportional to the square of the distance. So F' = 90·2/3² = 180/9 = 20 N.
quiz.1.q: Put the gravitational acceleration g in order from smallest to largest.
quiz.1.ogeler.1: A height R above Earth's surface (r = 2R)
quiz.1.ogeler.2: Height of the space station (≈ 400 km)
quiz.1.e: On the Moon g is about 1.6 m/s². At r = 2R, g drops to one quarter, about 2.45 m/s². On the space station g is about 8.7 m/s², and at Earth's surface it is about 9.8 m/s².
quiz.2.q: The orbital radius of a satellite around the same planet is made 4 times larger. How many times longer is its orbital period?
quiz.2.e: By Kepler's third law, T²/r³ is constant. When r is 4 times larger, T² is 4³ = 64 times larger and T is √64 = 8 times longer.
quiz.3.q: Two satellites move in circular orbits of the same radius. One has twice the mass of the other. What can you say about their orbital speeds?
quiz.3.o.0: The heavier one is 2 times faster
quiz.3.o.1: The heavier one is √2 times faster
quiz.3.e: The satellite's mass does not appear in v = √(G·M/r). The speed depends only on the planet's mass and the orbital radius.
quiz.3.y.0: Orbital speed is v = √(GM/r). The satellite's own mass is not in the formula.
quiz.3.y.1: The satellite's mass appears in both the gravitational force and the inertia, so it cancels. There is no √2 difference.
quiz.3.y.2: A lighter satellite does not move faster. At the same radius, the speed depends only on the planet's mass.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Tune gravity with mass and distance, put the ball into orbit, and cut the elevator cable.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Double the distance. Then set B's mass and bring the force back to F₀.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: When the distance doubles, the force drops to one part in 2² = 4. Making the mass 4 times larger brings the force back to F₀. This is called the inverse-square law.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.ipucu: First set the distance to 2 and see what fraction the force drops to.
A:adimlar.1.baslik: The apple pulls on Earth too
A:adimlar.1.metin: A 100 g apple falls from a tree. Earth pulls on the apple with about 1 N.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: How hard does the apple pull on Earth?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Every object with mass attracts. Being small does not make the force disappear.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Action and reaction forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The forces are equal. What is small is Earth's acceleration, not the force.
A:adimlar.2.baslik: g gets smaller as you rise
A:adimlar.2.metin: An 80 kg astronaut rises above the ground. Bring the astronaut's weight down to about 87 N.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: At 12 800 km up, r = 3R and g drops to one part in 3² = 9 (about 1.09 m/s²). The weight is 784 / 9 ≈ 87 N. The mass is still 80 kg.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: For the weight to drop to one ninth, the distance from the center must triple.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Watch the planet for one full trip around its elliptical orbit.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: Its speed is always the same
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Close to the Sun, gravity is stronger and the planet speeds up.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: It is slowest at aphelion. It has to move slowly so that the area swept in equal times stays the same.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Close to the Sun, the radius is short. To sweep the same area in the same time, the planet has to move faster.
A:adimlar.4.metin: A ball thrown horizontally from a mountaintop both falls and moves forward. If you throw it fast enough, the surface curves away beneath it. Put the ball into orbit.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: A ball thrown at about 7.9 km/s goes around Earth. A satellite is always falling too, but it keeps missing Earth. Gravity acts as the centripetal force, and v = √(GM/r).
A:adimlar.4.gorev.ipucu: Raise the speed a little above 7.9 km/s and press play.
A:adimlar.5.metin: If you raise the speed even more, the orbit stretches out. Free the ball from Earth's gravity.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: The escape velocity from Earth's surface is about 11.2 km/s, which is √2 times the orbital speed (7.9 × 1.41). An object thrown at this speed never comes back.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.ipucu: Escape velocity is about 1.41 times the orbital speed.
A:adimlar.6.metin: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator, and the scale reads 588 N. Cut the cable and press play.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: The person and the scale fall freely together, and the scale reads 0. Gravity is still there. It is the very reason they are falling.
A:kapanis.0: Any two masses attract each other, and F = G·m₁·m₂ / r². When the distance doubles, the force drops to one quarter.
A:kapanis.1: Gravitational forces are equal and opposite. The apple also pulls on Earth with 1 N.
A:kapanis.2: Since g = GM/r², it gets smaller as you rise. At r = 2R, g is one quarter of 9.8.
A:kapanis.3: Planets sweep equal areas in equal times and speed up near the Sun.
A:kapanis.4: Orbital speed is about 7.9 km/s and escape velocity is about 11.2 km/s. Satellites and astronauts are always falling.
